P1.evidence: The application was acknowledged but dismissed rather than reflected — "I saw your application but it's uh there's not not much information over there" — though he did come back to it later to confirm two facts ("you're 37, correct?" and "I saw that in the application, you wrote your marketing director"). No four-part frame and no frame agreement. The open question ran cleanly and in the script's own shape: "walk me through what's been going on with you in terms of fitness health and like what's the main thing that you're trying to fix right now."

P2.evidence: The injury work is the best in the batch and it is what determined the outcome. He asked, then kept asking: "What's up with the knee that you need the surgery?", "so when's that?", "Any other, apart, any other injuries that I need to be aware of?", "apart from the injuries, do you have any other kind of stiffness, like you mentioned, lower back, anything in the hips, in your traps, anywhere?", and then chased the surgical timeline — "do you anticipate what's the timeframe of that?" Work, training week, diet, sleep and energy all asked directly, with a genuinely sharp energy question that connected to the medication: "in terms of your energy levels, because I have, I had a few guys when they were on SSRI." Against that: age was confirmed rather than asked and height was never taken (weight only surfaced because the prospect volunteered the 182-to-189 change); health conditions were never asked, so the SSRI came out on its own inside a nutrition answer; and results from current training were never asked.

P3.evidence: The bridge question is the best-phrased in the whole batch, and it explicitly closed off the surface answer: "If you'd have put it like in your own words, what's your biggest why with this? Because don't tell me like you just want to get lean, yeah? That's not what I'm asking." It worked immediately — "it's honestly like mobility for the kids... the mobility and like energy to be able to play with them and like engage with them for like a longer period of time." Then nothing was built on it. No one-thing-you'd-change question, no mobility/strength/energy menu, no separate what-does-that-do-for-you, no who-else-does-this-impact, and the reflect-back never got past acknowledgement — "So we're playing the long-term game here" and "That adds up" rather than a full mirror with a tie-down. The kids were engaged earlier as biography ("two kids, one is one-year-old, correct?") rather than as a driver.

P4.evidence: The strongest move of the call and a better variant of P4f than the scripted line: "let me like, I don't understand yet, why do you need us? Why do you need Trevor?" It made the prospect argue the case himself and he named the gap unprompted — "I could go and just build my own program, find a program, buy it, stick to it. So I think it's the accountability piece... appreciated the accountability aspect of having somebody to check in. And track progress, track form." The consistency question then ran properly — "Do you think there's anything that's been keeping you from being consistent on this?" — and produced a clean self-diagnosis of the sleep-energy-window loop, which the rep mirrored back accurately. Weak points: no inventory of what he has actually tried and no follow-up on what happened with the previous online trainer.

P5.evidence: The rep decided at about the thirteen-minute mark not to proceed to an offer on this call because of the pending MRI and probable surgery, so the consequence frame — which exists to set up a close — had nothing to set up. Marked N/A rather than miss because the decision to stop was deliberate and correct, not an omission. Worth recording separately that this rep ran no consequence frame in any of the five sales calls in this batch, including the three where he did present a price.

P6.evidence: Not reachable. The commitment check precedes presenting, and nothing was presented — the rep closed the conversation with "let's schedule the call next week, and we'll pick it up from there."

P11.evidence: No close was attempted and no price was ever stated.

objection_plays.detail: This is the playbook's first known gap — a clinical-fit and clinical-timing situation with no scripted path — and it is the one instance in the corpus where the improvisation went the right way. The prospect had been told two days earlier that he needs knee surgery, with an MRI pending and four to six weeks on crutches expected. There is no play for this, and the rep neither ignored it nor sold around it. He named the problem out loud ("when you have MRI next week and it's going to turn out that, okay, you're going to be in surgery in two weeks, that's not enough time to prepare you"), declined to start him ("I don't see starting just for two weeks and then pausing"), described the injury-pause policy accurately, kept the prehab door open for a longer timeline ("if the surgery is going to be like in two months or three months, that's definitely a period that you can prepare yourself to actually recover faster"), and booked a follow-up two hours after the scan. The gap that remains is that nothing in the process required any of this — it was judgement, not procedure, and the prospect rather than the rep was the one who raised asking the surgeon about exercise.

notes: Short, well-diagnosed, and correctly stopped. The "why do you need Trevor?" question and the gated why question are both worth lifting into the script as written. The gap to coach is P3 depth — the best bridge question in the batch produced a real answer about his kids' mobility and then nothing was done with it — and the structural point for the principal is that this rep's good clinical judgement here had no procedural support behind it: there is still no intake question about health conditions, and clearance was never sought.
